Senses.PreferredTarget: life and death is the great matter
AlternateTargets: the matter of life and death is great
life and death, the great matter
the great matter of life and death
Senses.Explanation: (生) birth + (死) death + (事) matter/affair + (大) great: "life and death is the great matter." In the corpus it is overwhelmingly a fixed four-graph line, and in 84 places across 56 allowlist texts it stands in the paired form "life and death is the great matter; impermanence is swift" (生死事大，無常迅速); (無常迅速) itself occurs 160 times, 76 of them outside the pair. One text names the pair for what it is — "...two ready-made phrases" (生死事大，無常迅速，兩句現話, J28nB208). The attested deployment range is observable and wide: (i) as the reason for leaving home or seeking a teacher — (念生死事大) (19×) and (為生死事大) (39×), as in (念生死事大)，(奮志尋師) and (念生死事大)，(乃薙染完具) (X82n1571); (ii) as a plea addressed to a master — "...I beg the master to save me" (問生死事大請師相救, 古尊宿語錄); (iii) as an inscription — the (續燈正統) biography of (雲棲蓮池袾宏大師) records "at seventeen... he kept writing the four graphs (生死事大) on his desk" (年十七，補邑庠，每書生死事大四字於案頭, X84n1583), and (弘覺忞禪師北遊集) records of the emperor's lodging that (堂門書)「(生死事大)」 ("the hall door bore ", J26nB180); (iv) as the opening of a (上堂) sermon — (上堂)：「(大眾)！(又是九月半也)，(生死事大)，(無常迅速) (J32nB273); (v) as a raised (示眾) with a directive — (天如和尚示眾云)：『(生死事大)。(諸禪德)！(須是將生死兩字貼在額頭上始得)。』 (" (生死事大)...you must paste the two graphs 'life and death' (生死) on your forehead", J25nB171). The most-cited setting is the Yongjia–Huineng exchange, narrated in many texts: (覺曰)：「(生死事大)，(無常迅速)。」(祖曰)：「(何不體取無生)，(了無速乎)？」 The graphs (大事因緣) / (一大事因緣) (the "one great matter," 699× / 415×) are a separate stock phrase. The texts assign (生死事大) no gloss beyond the literal reading of its graphs, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Corpus-wide sense (SenseKey null): 321 occurrences in 135 allowlist texts spanning the B, C, D, J, T and X canons and many independent masters and compilers — the multi-source gate is met many times over. (Counts are whole-file, tag-stripped with <note>/<rdg>/<orig> apparatus excluded; gate-2 recount, confirmed by two independent recounts.) Curated occurrences here are all narrated, raised, or biographical (a lamp record, a supplicant's plea, an inscription, a sermon opening, a raised 示眾), so MasterName is null; the Yongjia–Huineng exchange records the line as Yongjia Xuanjue's (永嘉玄覺) but is retold at third hand in every allowlist witness. The dominant collocate is (無常迅速); cross-ref (無常迅速) and (大事因緣).

Senses.Explanation: The graphs join 'birth or arising' (生) to 'circumstance or connection' (緣). Of a person, the phrase asks the circumstance or place from which that person comes. Dongshan asks Lingyun, 'where is your place of origin?' (闍黎生緣何處), and Lingyun answers that he is a man of Min. Dazhu is asked the same question and answers, 'the sun rises in the east; the moon sets in the west' (日出東，月落西). Huanglong Huinan bends this ordinary origin question into one of his three chamber checkpoints: 'everyone has a place of origin; where is yours?' (人人盡有生緣，上座生緣在何處). His biography says the monasteries called the set Huanglong's Three Checkpoints. Later records quote, versify, appraise, and answer the same question. One later exchange answers 'face to face, you do not recognize it' (覿面不識), then explicitly asks what happens beyond the three checkpoints. These are different answers and institutional deployments of the same origin question, not additional lexical senses.
Senses.Note: The earlier draft split Huanglong's checkpoint from biographical 'native place.' Item 8 requires their merger: both ask the person's origin circumstance, and the named chamber setting changes deployment rather than referent. The generative condition applied to the myriad things remains separate below.

Senses.Explanation: In expository prose, the same graphs can name that by which things arise. Hongzhi says that what extends broadly throughout the domain and impartially like spring 'is the condition of arising of the myriad things' (箇是萬法之生緣也). The referent is a generative condition applying to the myriad things, not a person's birthplace or the origin question used in Huanglong's chamber.
Senses.Note: The predicate 'of the myriad things' establishes a different referent mechanically. One exact source currently anchors it, so the sense remains allowed rather than promoted to multi-source.

Occurrences.Kwic: 浩然遍域內。無私如陽春。箇是萬法之生緣也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi's hall discourse calls the impartial spring-like reach 'the condition of arising of the myriad things.'

Senses.Explanation: An imperative made from “quickly” and “say.” In Chan public interviews it presses the person addressed to produce an answer at once. The formula is often doubled—“Speak, quickly! Speak, quickly!”—and appears after a question, after alternatives have been barred, or with “bring forth” to demand the reply. The records place bodily consequences directly around it: a master holds a fork at a monk's neck, a monk pulls the master from the seat, or a staff beating follows. Other occurrences put it in a monk's request, “please, Master, answer quickly.” Its distinctive Chan use is timed pressure for an answer in a public interview; the phrase denotes the demand itself.
Senses.Note: Speaker direction changes—master to monk or monk to master—but the imperative denotes the same act, so no sense split is warranted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 道得也叉下死。道不得也叉下死。速道。速道。學徒鮮有對者
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The demand is doubled while a fork is held at the addressee's neck: whether he can speak or cannot, the case says death follows.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大悲千手眼那箇是正眼速道速道麻谷拽師下座

Occurrences.Kwic: 併却咽喉唇吻，速道將來。溈山出眾云：某甲道不得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The assembly is told to close throat and lips yet “bring forth [an answer], quickly”; Guishan steps out and says he cannot speak it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不得下語，不得無語。速道！速道！僧曰：請和尚放下竹篦
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the bamboo-comb case, both giving words and remaining wordless are barred before the doubled demand; the monk asks the master to put the comb down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不凡不聖請師速道田云老僧秪与麼師便喝
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Here a visitor asks the master to answer quickly concerning “neither ordinary nor holy”; the exchange continues with the master's words and a shout.
